big_idea: Leadership is an act of everyday influence available to anyone, regardless of formal position, what Sanborn calls leadership with a little l, and it's demonstrated through consistent behavior, not authority.

tool.label: The Six Practices of Little L Leadership
tool.text: Sanborn outlines six practices anyone can apply without a title: Self-Mastery, leading yourself first by clarifying your own purpose; Focus, intentionally prioritizing rather than drifting; Power With People, achieving goals through collaboration rather than command; Persuasive Communication, prioritizing being understood over simply transmitting information; Execution, turning ideas into consistent action; and Giving, making things better for others as a way of making things better for yourself.

ideas.title: Little l vs. Big L leadership
ideas.text: Formal, titled authority is only one form of leadership; everyday influence anyone can exercise is available regardless of rank.

ideas.title: Self-mastery first
ideas.text: You must lead yourself, clarify your own values and purpose, before you can credibly influence anyone else.

ideas.title: Power with, not power over
ideas.text: Effective influence comes from collaboration and shared purpose, not command-and-control authority.

ideas.title: Communication as understanding, not transmission
ideas.text: The goal of communicating isn't to have spoken, it's to have been genuinely understood by the other person.

ideas.title: Execution as active practice
ideas.text: Sanborn treats vision as a continuous verb, something practiced daily, rather than a static statement made once.

ideas.title: Legacy through giving
ideas.text: The book frames leadership's ultimate measure as the positive difference left in other people's lives, not formal recognition or career status.

try_it: Pick one interaction this week where you have no formal authority and practice power with, ask for input and build a shared plan instead of directing the outcome.
Before your next presentation or email, rewrite one sentence to prioritize whether the reader will understand it, not just whether it's technically correct.
Identify one small, specific way you can make someone else's day or work easier this week, without being asked.
Spend 15 minutes writing down your own definition of why you lead, independent of your job title.
best_for: Individual contributors or early-career professionals who want to build influence without waiting for a promotion
Anyone leading volunteers, peers, or informal groups
less_useful: The six practices are broad and motivational rather than tactically detailed, so readers wanting specific frameworks may find it thinner than more process-driven leadership books
At roughly 100 pages it's light on depth for readers wanting an in-depth treatment of any single practice

related.why: A complementary manifesto on leading a group of people who share a belief, with or without a title
A deeper look at the self-knowledge this book's self-mastery practice depends on

sources.label: Mark Sanborn: You Don't Need a Title to Be a Leader
